entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. Teacher plays a short audio clip of various toy sounds, such as a bouncing ball and a racing car, to capture students' attention.
2. Teacher asks students like Muhammad Firdaus Alfandi to identify the sounds and share how they feel when they hear them.
3. Teacher introduces the topic "My Favourite Things" and explains the objective of learning new vocabulary today.

 

Lesson Development

Vocabulary and Sentence Frame Introduction

1. Teacher displays flashcards of common toys and models the pronunciation of words like robot, doll, and kite.
2. Teacher introduces the sentence frame "My favourite thing is my (toy)" on the whiteboard.
3. Students like Muslimahtul Ramadani participate in choral repetition to build confidence in using the new vocabulary.

 

Pair Interview Practice

1. Teacher provides a simple interview guide with the question "What is your favourite thing?" and the response frame.
2. Nick Mikhael interviews Santhiya A/P Subramaniam by asking the question and listening to her response.
3. Students switch roles and record their partner's favourite item by drawing a small picture next to the name.
4. Teacher moves around the classroom to provide scaffolding and correct pronunciation for the weaker learners.

 

Small Group Memory Discussion

1. Teacher divides the class into small groups and gives each group a task card with pictures of five different items.
2. Muhamad Harith Aqasha leads his group to memorise the items for one minute before the card is turned over.
3. Group members take turns saying "I remember the (item)" and then discuss which of those items they like best.
4. Each group shares their favourite item from the card with the rest of the class to practice public speaking.

 

Post-lesson

1. Teacher invites Nur Dayana Qhairena to summarise the lesson by naming one thing she learned to say today.
2. Riszuwan Haiqal and other students add to the summary by listing other favourite things mentioned during the activities.
entries.reflection_html: The lesson was successful as the students enjoyed the audio-based induction and the memory task. Nur'Irish Zara Amna showed significant progress in using the sentence frames, while Muhammad Thaqif Danial demonstrated good leadership during the group discussion.

entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. Teacher plays a short 30-second audio clip of a child excitedly talking about receiving a new teddy bear for their birthday.
2. Teacher asks Muhamad Harith Aqasha and Muhammad Firdaus Alfandi how the child in the audio feels and why they sound so happy.
3. Teacher introduces the lesson topic 'My Favourite Things' and explains that they will read about what other children love.

 

Lesson Development

Vocabulary and Sentence Scaffolding

1. Teacher introduces key vocabulary: 'robot', 'storybook', 'bicycle', 'shiny', and 'fast' using picture cards.
2. Teacher conducts choral repetition of the words to ensure correct pronunciation.
3. Teacher introduces sentence frames on the board: 'My favourite thing is a...', 'It is [color/size]', and 'I like it because it is...'.

 

Jigsaw Reading: Friends and Their Toys

1. Teacher divides the class into three home groups: Group A, B, and C.
2. Group A reads Text 1: 'Ali has a red robot. It is small and fast. He plays with it in the garden.'
3. Group B reads Text 2: 'Sara has a big storybook. It has many colorful pictures. She reads it before bed.'
4. Group C reads Text 3: 'Ben has a blue bicycle. It is very shiny. He rides it to the park with his dad.'
5. Students move to expert groups to discuss their specific text, then return to home groups to teach their teammates what they read using the sentence frames.

 

Info-Gap: Finding the Matching Item

1. Students work in pairs, such as Muslimahtul Ramadani and Nick Mikhael bin Hendra Cipta.
2. Student A receives a worksheet with pictures of a green ball and a yellow kite but no names; Student B receives descriptions: 'The green ball is round' and 'The yellow kite is high'.
3. Student B reads the description aloud while Student A listens and writes the correct name under each picture.
4. Teacher monitors Muhammad Syahir Haikal and Muhammad Thaqif Danial, providing extra guidance with the reading prompts.
5. Pairs swap roles with a new set of items (a purple doll and a brown drum) to practice both reading and listening.

 

Post-lesson

1. Teacher asks students to complete a '3-2-1' exit ticket: write 3 new words learned, 2 questions about the story characters, and 1 opinion on which toy was the best.
2. Nur Dayana Qhairena shares her opinion with the class, stating why she prefers the storybook over the bicycle.
entries.reflection_html: Muhamad Harith Aqasha showed good progress in identifying the main idea of the short passage. Muslimahtul Ramadani and Nick Mikhael bin Hendra Cipta successfully completed the info-gap task with minimal teacher intervention, showing improved confidence in reading simple sentences.

entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. Teacher shows a zoomed-in, blurred mystery image of a colorful gift box and asks students like Muhammad Firdaus Alfandi to predict what the object is.
2. Teacher slowly reveals the full image of the gift and elicits the word 'present' or 'gift' from the class through choral repetition.
3. Teacher asks the class how they feel when they get a gift and explains they will learn to write a simple thank-you card today.

 

Lesson Development

Parts of a Simple Thank-You Card

1. Teacher displays a large sample thank-you card on the board with three clear sections: 'To:', 'Thank you for the...', and 'From:'.
2. Teacher uses a pointer to show each section and asks the class to repeat the labels loudly.
3. Teacher models filling in the blanks using a simple gift like 'ball' or 'doll' to show how the sentence frame works.

 

Gift Interview Pair Work

1. Students are paired up to conduct a simple Q&A interview about their favourite gifts using a provided question card.
2. Nur Amni Awatif asks her partner 'What is your favourite gift?' and listens for the answer to help them choose a word for their card.
3. Teacher monitors the pairs, helping students like Nick Mikhael to spell simple words such as 'robot' or 'book' for their drafts.

 

Group Task Card Brainstorming

1. Students sit in small groups and receive a task card featuring a picture of a common gift like a bicycle or a teddy bear.
2. Muhammad Syahir Haikal and his group members discuss who they would give the card to, such as 'Mom' or 'Dad'.
3. Each student writes a draft of their thank-you card on a worksheet, using the group's task card as a visual reference for vocabulary.

 

Post-lesson

1. Teacher asks students to look at their completed thank-you cards and think about which part was the easiest to write and which part was the hardest.
2. Nur Dayana Qhairena shares her reflection with the class, explaining that writing her name was easy but spelling the gift name was a bit hard.
entries.reflection_html: The majority of the students were able to complete the thank-you card using the provided sentence frames. Muslimahtul Ramadani and Riszuwan Haiqal showed good progress in their writing skills by correctly identifying the recipient and the gift in their work.

entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. Teacher presents a scenario where a student named Ali feels constantly exhausted and struggles to focus during football practice due to a diet consisting solely of processed snacks and soda.
2. Teacher asks the class to identify the main problem with Ali's lifestyle and how it affects his physical performance.
3. Students provide immediate verbal suggestions to help Ali improve his energy levels through better food choices.

 

Lesson Development

Jigsaw Reading: The Power of Nutrients

1. Teacher divides the class into four expert groups, each receiving a different short text about Proteins, Carbohydrates, Vitamins, or Healthy Fats.
2. The Vitamin text explains: "Vitamins and minerals are essential for a strong immune system. Found in fruits like oranges and vegetables like spinach, they protect the body from getting sick easily. Without them, the body becomes weak and prone to infections."
3. Students like Muhammad Ammar Ziqri read their assigned text and highlight three specific benefits of their food group.
4. Students return to their home groups to teach their teammates about their specific nutrient, ensuring everyone understands why each group is necessary.
5. Teacher monitors the groups to ensure accurate information is being shared and clarifies any difficult vocabulary.

 

Task Card Challenge: The Healthy Menu Planner

1. Teacher distributes task cards to small groups, requiring them to design a one-day balanced meal plan for an athlete.
2. Groups must use connectors such as "consequently," "as a result," and "in order to" when justifying their food selections.
3. Kalvin Pillai leads his group in selecting complex carbohydrates over simple sugars, explaining that they provide longer-lasting energy.
4. Each group presents their menu orally to the class, defending their choices based on the facts learned in the jigsaw reading phase.
5. Peer feedback is given focusing on the clarity of the reasons provided for each healthy eating advice.

 

Post-lesson

1. Teacher conducts a quick-fire quiz where students give a thumbs-up if a statement about healthy eating is true and a thumbs-down if it is false.
2. Teacher asks Khayla Dhia Jannah to provide a brief spoken summary of why balance is the most important part of a healthy diet.
entries.reflection_html: The lesson was highly effective as Muhammad Ammar Ziqri and Kalvin Pillai successfully integrated complex connectors into their spoken justifications. Khayla Dhia Jannah also demonstrated a clear understanding of the nutrient groups during the final check, showing significant progress in speaking confidence.

entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. Teacher poses the provocative question: 'If you could live forever by only eating steamed broccoli and water, would you do it, or would you rather eat your favorite junk food and live a shorter life?'
2. Students like Kalvin Pillai and Ainnur Raudhah discuss their choices in pairs for two minutes, justifying their reasons using 'because' and 'due to'.
3. Teacher selects three students to share their partner's opinion with the class to transition into the topic of healthy eating.

 

Lesson Development

Complex Connectors in Nutrition Discussions

1. Teacher explains the use of connectors such as 'consequently', 'furthermore', and 'in contrast' when discussing health benefits.
2. Teacher provides examples of how these connectors link ideas in a food article about Mediterranean diets.
3. Teacher plays a short audio clip of the article's introduction for students to identify the speaker's main thesis.

 

Jigsaw Listening: Nutritional Components

1. Teacher divides the class into four 'Expert' groups: Proteins, Carbohydrates, Vitamins, and Healthy Fats.
2. Each group listens to a specific 1-minute audio segment detailing the benefits and sources of their assigned component.
3. Keerthikan and Khayla Dhia Jannah lead their expert groups to list three specific details heard in the recording.
4. Students reform into 'Home' groups where each member is an expert in a different component.
5. Each expert teaches their home group members what they learned while others fill in a graphic organizer.

 

The Healthy Recipe Info-Gap

1. Students work in pairs where Student A has the ingredients list for a 'Healthy Quinoa Salad' and Student B has the preparation steps, but both have missing information.
2. Muhammad Ammar Ziqri and Nur Adni Irdina must communicate orally to complete their respective sheets without looking at each other's papers.
3. Students must listen for specific quantities (e.g., 200g, 2 tablespoons) and action verbs (e.g., whisk, simmer) to complete the recipe.
4. Pairs verify their completed recipes against a master copy displayed on the board.

 

Post-lesson

1. Students perform the 3-2-1 activity: writing down 3 new vocabulary words related to food, 2 questions they have about nutrition, and 1 personal opinion on the 'steamed broccoli' debate.
2. Teacher collects the responses and provides immediate oral feedback on the common questions raised.
entries.reflection_html: Nur Zara Damia demonstrated excellent listening comprehension by accurately capturing the specific measurements during the info-gap activity. Low Mei Yik and Mohamad Aqil Fayyadh showed significant progress in using logical connectors when explaining the benefits of healthy fats to their peers.

entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. Teacher displays five True or False statements on the board regarding healthy habits in different countries, such as 'People in Japan eat a lot of sweet potatoes for long life.'
2. Students like Kalvin Pillai and Nur Adni Irdina must stand up if they think the statement is true or stay seated if they think it is false.
3. Teacher reveals the answers and briefly introduces the lesson focus on reading about healthy diets from various cultures.

 

Lesson Development

Understanding Cultural Diets

1. Teacher introduces a short reading passage: 'The Okinawan diet from Japan focuses on sweet potatoes and green vegetables, resulting in many people living over 100 years. Similarly, the Mediterranean diet emphasizes nuts, fish, and olive oil to protect the heart. Both cultures avoid processed sugars and prioritize fresh, local ingredients for every meal.'
2. Teacher highlights key connectors such as 'similarly' and 'both' to show how to compare different ideas.
3. Teacher explains the criteria for an effective healthy eating poster, focusing on clear advice and cultural references.

 

Info-Gap: Comparing Global Diets

1. Teacher divides the class into pairs where Student A receives a text about the Nordic diet and Student B receives a text about the Mexican diet.
2. Khayla Dhia Jannah and Mohamad Aqil FayYadh must interview their partners to find out which main ingredients and health benefits are specific to the other person's text.
3. Students complete a comparison table based only on the information provided by their partner's verbal description of their reading.

 

Simulation: The International Health Fair

1. Students are assigned to 'booths' representing different cultures and must simulate a health fair where they give advice to visitors.
2. Krettisha Nair and Muhammad Ammar Ziqri act as nutritionists, using their reading notes to advise 'visitors' on how to incorporate international healthy habits into a daily routine.
3. During the simulation, students sketch a draft of a healthy eating poster that combines advice from at least two different cultures.

 

Post-lesson

1. Students perform an individual reflection by writing on a small slip of paper one thing they found easy about the reading and one vocabulary word they found difficult.
2. Teacher collects the slips to identify which students might need more support with complex sentence structures in the next lesson.
entries.reflection_html: Low Mei Yik demonstrated a strong grasp of the Nordic diet details during the info-gap task, while Nur Zara Damia successfully used the connector 'similarly' when explaining food benefits during the health fair simulation.

entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. Teacher poses the provocative question: 'Can we truly judge a person's character based solely on their physical appearance, or are first impressions always misleading?'
2. Students like Afif Irsyaduddin and Auni think individually for one minute before discussing their perspectives with a partner, citing examples of people they know.
3. Teacher invites a few pairs to share their conclusions, bridging the discussion to the importance of listening for both physical and personality traits.

 

Lesson Development

Personality and Appearance Jigsaw Reading

1. Teacher divides the class into four 'Home' groups, each assigned a different short text describing a complex character's appearance and personality.
2. Ahmad Harraz and his group members read their specific text and summarize the main ideas, focusing on how the person's actions reflect their traits.
3. Students move to 'Expert' groups containing one member from each Home group to share their summaries orally.
4. Members in the Expert groups must listen carefully to their peers and fill in a comparison matrix for all four characters without reading the other texts.

 

The Mystery Witness Info-Gap

1. Students are paired up as Student A and Student B; Fatin Aqilah (Student A) receives a list of physical descriptions, while Javis Oh Wei Xiang (Student B) receives a list of personality profiles.
2. Student A describes a suspect's appearance using complex sentences, and Student B must listen to identify which personality profile in their list logically matches that person.
3. They exchange information using clarifying questions like 'Does his messy hair suggest he is disorganized?' to reach a consensus on the identity of three suspects.
4. Pairs present their final matches to the class, explaining the logic behind their choices based on the information they heard from their partners.

 

Post-lesson

1. Teacher asks the students to imagine these characters are involved in a mystery that needs solving in the next class.
2. Teacher hints that tomorrow they will use these descriptions to identify a 'secret culprit' hidden among the profiles they studied today.
entries.reflection_html: Ahmad Harraz and Auni demonstrated strong leadership during the jigsaw activity, helping their peers synthesize complex descriptions. Fatin Aqilah and Javis Oh Wei Xiang successfully completed the info-gap task with minimal teacher support, showing clear progress toward B1 listening and speaking targets.

entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. Students move around the classroom to view four different character mood boards featuring images and cryptic quotes about personality.
2. Students jot down one initial impression for each board on a sticky note and paste it next to the image.
3. Teacher calls on Lee Kok Sing and Fatin Aqilah to explain their word choices for the most mysterious-looking character.

 

Lesson Development

Jigsaw Character Analysis

1. Teacher assigns each student to an expert group to analyze one of four short literary excerpts describing a character's behavior and environment.
2. Litthika and her expert group read a passage about a character named Silas who mended every broken toy in the village but never smiled.
3. Students return to their original home groups and take turns presenting the traits they inferred from their specific text.
4. Javis Oh Wei Xiang ensures his group members record the evidence for each character trait discussed.

 

Character Trait Task Cards

1. Teacher provides each group with a task card featuring a paragraph about an old sea captain and asks them to determine his primary motivation.
2. Ahmad Harraz leads the group in identifying connectors in the text that link the captain's actions to his underlying personality traits.
3. Each group writes a three-sentence summary of the captain's character on a mini-whiteboard to present to the class.

 

Post-lesson

1. Teacher presents three scenarios of character behavior and asks students to give a thumbs up for reliable or thumbs down for unreliable.
2. Afif Irsyaduddin provides a verbal justification for the final scenario, linking it back to the vocabulary learned during the lesson.
entries.reflection_html: Lavanya and Muhammad Izzat demonstrated high-level inference skills during the jigsaw activity, successfully identifying traits not explicitly stated. The lesson successfully moved the A2 High students toward B1 proficiency by requiring evidence-based reasoning.

entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. Display a silhouette or partial photo of a famous person on the screen. Ask: "Who is this? How would you describe them?"
2. Elicit 3-4 describing words from students (e.g., tall, kind, famous). Write them on the board.
3. Tell students: "Today, you will write a full description of a person -- just like a character profile."

 

Lesson Development

Structure of a Character Description

1. Show a model paragraph describing a character (e.g. a teacher). Highlight four parts: name/introduction, appearance, personality, and interesting facts.
2. Point out connecting words: and, but, because, also. Circle reference pronouns: he, she, they, his, her.
3. Write sentence frames on the board: "He/She is ... because ...", "... also ...", "... but ...".
4. Ask Choye Kai En: "If you describe your best friend, what would you say first?" Then ask Auni: "What about personality words?"

 

Guided Writing -- Describe a Classmate

1. Pair students. Each pair chooses one person to describe (a classmate, a teacher, or a family member).
2. Provide a planning sheet with four sections: Name & Introduction, Appearance, Personality, Interesting Fact. Students jot 2-3 points per section.
3. Students write 1-2 paragraphs using the sentence frames and connectors. Target: at least 6 sentences with 2 coordinating conjunctions and 2 reference pronouns.
4. Circulate and give individual feedback. Check Afif Irsyaduddin's use of 'because' and Ahmad Harraz' pronoun consistency.
5. Early finishers add an extra sentence about 'What I admire about this person'.

 

Peer Review & Gallery Walk

1. Students swap papers with another pair. They read and underline: one colour for conjunctions, another for reference pronouns.
2. Each pair gives one positive comment and one suggestion for improvement.
3. Volunteers read their descriptions aloud. Class guesses who is being described based on the details.

 

Post-lesson

1. Recap: Ask 2-3 students to share one sentence from their description.
2. Quick quiz: Show 3 sentences with missing connectors/pronouns. Students complete orally.
3. Exit ticket: Write one sentence describing someone in your family using 'because'.
entries.reflection_html: Aayra Faiz Firman produced a very detailed character description with good use of 'and' and 'but' to connect ideas, showing strong B1 Low writing ability. Afif Irsyaduddin needed prompting to use reference pronouns consistently but improved after peer review feedback. The gallery walk activity was highly engaging. For next time, I will provide a checklist for weaker students to self-check their use of conjunctions and pronouns before submitting.

entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. Show 6-8 pictures of places in town (library, hospital, supermarket, park, bank, restaurant, school, police station).
2. Point to each picture and say: "What place is this?" Elicit the word. Correct pronunciation and repeat chorally.
3. Reveal students' worksheet for the lesson: a bingo card with the same 8 places in random positions.

 

Lesson Development

Places in Town Vocabulary

1. Display a map of a simple town on the screen with 8 labelled places.
2. Read each word aloud. Students repeat in chorus, then in pairs.
3. Match each word to a simple definition: "A place where you borrow books = ..." (library), "A place where you buy food = ..." (supermarket).
4. Ask Indah Sufiha: "Where do you go when you are sick?" Ask Adrieya Shahzuelia: "Where do you buy bread?"

 

Places Bingo Game

1. Give each student a bingo card with 9 squares (8 place names + 1 FREE square). Call out definitions one by one. Students mark the matching place.
2. First student to get 3 in a row shouts "Bingo!" and reads back their words. Teacher checks accuracy.
3. Play 3 rounds. Between rounds, shuffle vocabulary on the board so students cannot predict.
4. For students struggling (e.g. Mohamad Hazim Daniel), point to the word on the board and say the definition again slowly.

 

Match the Place -- Worksheet

1. Worksheet with two columns: Column A has 8 place pictures, Column B has 8 short descriptions. Students draw lines to match.
2. Students complete individually. Teacher circulates, providing word banks for weaker students.
3. Review answers as a class. Each student reads one match aloud.

 

Post-lesson

1. Students close their books. Teacher says a place name, students mime an action associated with that place (e.g. library = quiet finger to lips).
2. Recap: "Which place is easiest to remember? Which is hardest?"
3. Exit ticket: Write the name of 3 places in town from today's lesson.
entries.reflection_html: Indah Sufiha struggled with pronouncing 'supermarket' and 'restaurant' but successfully matched pictures to definitions with one-on-one support. Izz Rayyan Arasy was the first bingo winner and helped classmates by pointing to words on the board. The bingo game was very effective for vocabulary retention -- nearly all students could identify all 8 places by the end of the lesson. Next lesson I will introduce full sentences ('I go to the library to borrow books') to bridge vocabulary to speaking.

entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. Display a simple town map on screen with places labelled (library, hospital, park, school, supermarket, bank).
2. Say: "I am at the school. I want to go to the library. Which way?" Trace the route on the map with your finger.
3. Introduce directional phrases: turn left, turn right, go straight, next to, between, opposite.

 

Lesson Development

Reading Directions -- Key Phrases

1. Write 6 direction phrases on the board with simple diagrams (arrows showing left, right, straight).
2. Model a simple direction: "Start at the school. Go straight. Turn right at the supermarket. The library is next to the cafe."
3. Students repeat each direction sentence as a class.
4. Ask Izzara Safiya: "Where is the hospital on this map?" Ask Mohamad Hazim Daniel: "What is next to the bank?"

 

Read and Colour the Route

1. Give each student a worksheet with a map of Small Town (8 places, simple grid layout).
2. Three direction passages are printed below the map. Students read each passage and draw the route in a different colour on the map.
3. Passages are short (2-3 sentences each): e.g. "Start at the park. Go straight. Turn left at the library. The bank is on your right."
4. After drawing, students write the final destination in the blank: "You arrive at the _____".
5. Teacher works closely with weak readers. Provide word bank with place pictures on the worksheet border.

 

Partner Direction Reading

1. Pairs. Student A has Map A, Student B has Map B (different starting points).
2. Student A reads a direction. Student B traces it on their map and says the destination.
3. Swap roles after 3 directions each.

 

Post-lesson

1. Display one direction phrase. Students point left/right/wrong to show understanding of the direction.
2. Quick review: "Which direction phrase was new today?" "Where is the library from the school?"
3. Exit ticket: Draw a simple arrow and label it with turn left, turn right, or go straight.
entries.reflection_html: Izzara Safiya confidently identified places on the map and helped her partner Adriesya Shahzuelia during the partner reading activity. Mohamad Hazim Daniel needed extra support with 'opposite' and 'between' but could follow 'go straight' and 'turn left' independently. The colour-coding of routes made the reading task more accessible for weak readers. Next lesson, I will reduce text length for the lowest group and add picture-supported directions for A1-level students.

entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. Show a simple town guide from a tourist brochure or an example you wrote. Read it aloud.
2. Ask: "If a visitor comes to our town, what places should they visit?" Brainstorm 4-5 places on the board.
3. Tell students: "Today, you will write a short town guide to help a visitor know where to go."

 

Lesson Development

What is a Town Guide?

1. Show a model town guide (3-4 sentences): "Welcome to Small Town. You can visit the library to read books. The park is great for playing. The supermarket sells food. Enjoy your stay!"
2. Highlight the sentence pattern: You can visit/see/find [place] to [activity/verb].
3. Point out the opening sentence (Welcome to...) and closing sentence (Enjoy your stay / Have fun).
4. Ask Izz Rayyan Arasy: "What sentence could we write about the park?" Ask Indah Sufiha: "What can you do at the hospital?" (guide them if stuck).

 

Guided Writing -- Our Town Guide

1. Give each student a planning frame with sentence starters: "Welcome to _____! You can visit _____ to _____. The _____ is a good place for _____. Have a great time in _____!"
2. Students fill in the blanks using the places from the word bank on the board (8 places from the week).
3. Target: 5-6 complete sentences. Use at least 3 different places.
4. Teacher circulates. Help weaker students (e.g. Mohamad Hazim Daniel, Adriesya Shahzuelia) with vocabulary and sentence structure by pointing to the word bank and modelling one sentence at a time.
5. Early finishers add one more sentence with 'You can also...'

 

Share Your Guide

1. Students read their town guide to a partner. Partner gives one like and one question.
2. Select 3-4 volunteers to read their guide to the class.
3. Display guides on the board for peer recognition.

 

Post-lesson

1. Recap the structure: opening, places with activities, closing.
2. Ask: "Which part was hardest?" Students show fingers: 1=opening, 2=activities, 3=closing.
3. Exit ticket: Write one sentence recommending your favourite place in town.
entries.reflection_html: Izz Rayyan Arasy wrote a complete town guide with 6 sentences independently, including a creative closing line about enjoying local food. Mohamad Hazim Daniel needed sentence-by-sentence scaffolding but successfully completed the guided writing frame with 4 out of 5 sentences correct. The planning frame reduced writing anxiety for weaker students. Next lesson I will extend this to include 'why' statements ('You should visit the park because it is beautiful') to challenge the handful of students ready for more complexity.

entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. Play a 30-second audio clip of street sounds (music, crowd cheering, typing sounds, a radio commentary). Ask: "What is happening? What could the person's job or hobby be?"
2. Elicit hobby and career words related to the sounds (musician, singer, office worker, reporter).
3. Tell students: "Today, we will listen to short talks about people's hobbies and the careers they dream of."

 

Lesson Development

Listening for Specific Details

1. Pre-teach 5 key words/phrases from the listening text: talent show, audition, passion, career path, stage fright.
2. Students repeat each word. Match to pictures/short definitions on the board.
3. Set the listening task: "You will hear three teenagers talking about their hobbies and dream careers. Listen for: name, hobby, dream job, one reason."
4. Ask Amsyar: "What was the first word we learned?" Ask Aliff Fahmii: "What does 'passion' mean?"

 

Listening Task -- Hobbies & Dream Careers

1. Play Audio Track 1 (teenager A -- hobby: playing guitar, dream: music producer). Students fill in a table: Name, Hobby, Dream Career, Reason.
2. Pause after Track 1. Check answers with whole class. Clarify any missed details.
3. Play Track 2 (teenager B -- hobby: baking, dream: pastry chef). Students complete second row of the table.
4. Play Track 3 (teenager C -- hobby: coding games, dream: software developer). Students complete third row.
5. Students compare answers with a partner before class review.

 

Talent Show Discussion

1. In groups of 3-4, students discuss: "If our class had a talent show, what hobby would you show? Could it become a career?"
2. Provide discussion frames: "My hobby is ___ and I could show ___ in a talent show.", "This could become a career because ___ ."
3. Each group shares one interesting idea with the class.
4. Ask Aqilah Hasnaa': "What hobby would you show?" Ask Azwa Shahirah: "Could that become a career? Why?"

 

Post-lesson

1. Recap: In one sentence, say one hobby-career connection from today.
2. Dictation: Read 2 sentences from the audio. Students write what they hear.
3. Exit ticket: Write your hobby and one career that connects to it.
entries.reflection_html: Ahmad Amsyar accurately identified all three dream careers from the listening text and was the first to connect 'coding' to 'software developer' during class discussion. Areej Az Zahra produced an excellent opinion during group discussion, using 'because' to explain why baking could lead to a career as a pastry chef. The listening table task kept all students focused and accountable. Next lesson, I will use a more extended monologue (30-40 seconds) to push listening stamina for the strongest B1 Low students.

entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. Teacher displays four images around the classroom representing different career paths: a professional chef, a software developer, a wildlife photographer, and a commercial pilot.
2. Students, including Aliff Fahmii and Areej Az Zahra, perform a gallery walk to observe the images and write one hobby that might lead to each career on sticky notes.
3. Teacher facilitates a brief discussion linking the students' hobby suggestions to the lesson's focus on career profiles and key details.

 

Lesson Development

Career Profile Info-Gap

1. Teacher divides the class into pairs, assigning Student A and Student B roles to each pair.
2. Student A receives a profile of 'Sarah the Marine Biologist' which describes her background and hobbies: Sarah is a Marine Biologist based in Sabah. She has always loved scuba diving and exploring coral reefs since she was young. Her hobby of underwater photography helps her document rare species.
3. Student B receives Sarah's daily work tasks: She spends her mornings collecting water samples for analysis. In the afternoon, she tags sea turtles to track their migration patterns. She also writes reports for the local conservation department.
4. Students like Lohsheny and Mithish Raj must ask each other specific questions to complete a full profile worksheet without looking at their partner's paper.
5. Pairs verify their completed profiles to ensure they have correctly identified all key details from the reading text.

 

Career Consultant Simulation

1. Teacher explains how to match personal hobbies to professional requirements using vocabulary such as 'analytical skills' and 'technical expertise'.
2. Students engage in a simulation where one student acts as a client listing three hobbies, and the other acts as a consultant.
3. Natalie Tan and Ng Min Hyn take turns recommending careers based on the profiles read earlier, providing two reasons for their choice.
4. Students must refer back to the key details in the career profiles to justify why a specific hobby makes a candidate suitable for the role.
5. The 'consultants' write a final three-sentence recommendation for their client to practice paragraph-level output.

 

Post-lesson

1. Teacher invites Muhammad Yusuf Imran to stand and summarize the main connections found between hobbies and career profiles today.
2. Azwa Shahirah and other classmates add further details or differing opinions to the summary to ensure a comprehensive wrap-up of the learning objective.
entries.reflection_html: 1. The info-gap activity successfully challenged Lohsheny and Mithish Raj to use specific reading strategies to find missing information. 2. Natalie Tan and Ng Min Hyn demonstrated high-level critical thinking during the simulation by effectively linking hobbies to career demands. 3. Most students achieved the learning standard, though a few required more prompting to expand their justifications into full paragraphs.

entries.activity_html:
Set Induction

1. Display a photo of a famous person (e.g. Michelle Yeoh, Yusof Ishak, or a local figure). Ask: "Who is this? What is their job? What hobby might they have had as a child?"
2. Elicit 2-3 ideas. Transition: "Stories about people often show how hobbies become careers. Today we will read about characters and connect their stories to our own lives."
3. Write the LO on the board: "Connect career and hobby stories to personal experiences."

 

Lesson Development

Making Text-to-Self Connections

1. Read aloud a short biographical passage (e.g. a 6-sentence story about a young person who turned their love of drawing into an animation career).
2. Model a text-to-self connection: "In this story, the person loved drawing as a child. I also liked drawing. When I was young, I drew cartoons. This story reminds me of..."
3. Write connection sentence frames: "This reminds me of...", "I also...", "I feel the same because...", "Unlike the character, I...".
4. Ask Areej Az Zahra: "Does this story remind you of any hobby you have?" Ask Aqilah Hasnaa': "Can you finish the sentence: 'I also...'?"

 

Read & Connect -- Career Stories

1. Provide each pair with one of three short passages (differentiated):
- Text A (higher): A teen who turned football practice into a coaching career
- Text B (mid): A girl who loved cooking and became a chef
- Text C (support): A boy who liked fixing things and became a mechanic
2. Students read their passage. Use a 3-column graphic organizer: What happened in the story? / What hobby/career is this? / How does this connect to my life?
3. Students complete the organizer individually, then share with their partner.
4. Teacher circulates. Ask Aliff Fahmii: "How does the football story connect to you?" Ask Ahmad Amsyar: "What about the cooking story -- have you ever helped cook at home?"

 

Group Sharing & Class Connection Web

1. Each group shares one strong text-to-self connection from their passage.
2. Teacher draws a 'connection web' on the board: write passage titles in circles, connect them with student names who shared similar experiences.
3. Class votes on the most surprising or interesting connection.

 

Post-lesson

1. Recap: "What does 'text-to-self connection' mean in your own words?"
2. Quick write: In 2-3 sentences, answer: "If you could turn a hobby into a career, what would it be and why?"
3. Exit ticket: Write one sentence starting with 'This reminds me of...'
entries.reflection_html: Aqilah Hasnaa' made a thoughtful connection between the cooking passage and helping her mother prepare meals at home, using the sentence frame 'I also...' with confidence. Ahmad Amsyar connected the football story to his own experience as a school athlete and produced a three-sentence written reflection with B1-level complexity. The differentiated texts ensured every student could access the material at their level. Next lesson I will introduce text-to-text connections (comparing two career stories) to push the stronger groups further.
